title: Hosting Phonotype Architectures and Runbook
body:
Purpose:
This note captures a compact, pragmatic playbook for selecting and sequencing hosting options for customer POCs. It is intentionally prescriptive: the goal is to give a SE (solutions engineering) team a repeatable flow that balances time-to-first-demo, measurable risk, and operational overhead.

Context and audience:
- Audience: SEs running customer workshops and internal engineers helping with capacity and SRE handoff.
- Typical POC profile this covers: mid-market SaaS or enterprise app integrating a high-throughput conversational endpoint (qps 20-200 across peak windows) with moderate sensitive data (PII present in prompts) and strict latency targets for UI interactions (p95 target <= 350ms).

High-level decision dimensions (what drives architecture choice):
1) Data sovereignty and compliance (can user data leave customer network?).
2) Latency envelope and geographic distribution.
3) Predictability of throughput vs. bursty peaks.
4) Integration surface (direct API calls vs. private network connections).
5) Customer appetite for ops vs. desire for managed experience.
6) Cost sensitivity and procurement timelines.

Customer archetypes and recommended starting posture:
- Fast PLG proof-of-value (no regulatory barriers): Start hosted. Rationale: fastest time-to-first-result, lowest ops friction, easiest to iterate on prompts and model selection.
- Regulated enterprise (data residency or strict audits): Start private (VPC or on-prem) or dedicated with network peering. Rationale: certs, KMS integration, audit controls.
- High throughput with tight latency and partial data restrictions: Hybrid (dedicated + edge cache) to keep hot paths local and fall back to hosted variants.

Phonotype architectures (practical, repeatable groupings)
1) Hosted-first (fast path)
   - Components: Redwood hosted API (model catalog), customer front-end, optional token-level telemetry enabled.
   - Integration: API key, optional IP allowlist.
   - When to choose: exploratory POC, short timelines (< 2 weeks), low legal friction.
   - Pros: rapid demo, online tooling (console), lowest ops.
   - Cons: limited custom networking, must address data residency contractual questions.

2) Dedicated-reserved (predictable throughput)
   - Components: Dedicated GPU pool, reserved capacity, route policy in smart routing to land requests on dedicated cluster.
   - Integration: VPC peering or customer IP egress; SLA contract.
   - When to choose: predictable steady throughput, enterprise customers requiring SLA.
   - Pros: performance predictability, stronger isolation, configurable autoscale/burst.
   - Cons: cost commit, longer provisioning timeline (days-weeks).

3) Private (VPC-hosted or on-prem)
   - Components: Private control plane, customer-managed compute or Redwood appliance, KMS/HSM integration, audit logging to customer SIEM.
   - Integration: Direct private connectivity, CICD to customer infra.
   - When to choose: data residency, legal/regulatory requirements, air-gapped environments.
   - Pros: maximum control, compliance-friendly.
   - Cons: highest ops burden, longer sales/implementation cycle.

4) Hybrid patterns (common mixes)
   - Edge-cache + Hosted fallthrough: prefix caching for repeated prompts, local inference layer for short responses, hosted fallback for rare/long responses. Good for latency-critical UI with predictable repetitive queries.
   - Split by workload: embeddings/summarization on dedicated/private (data sensitive), creative generation on hosted. Useful when parts of pipeline differ in sensitivity and cost profile.
   - Active-active regional placement + central hosted catalog: for geo-distributed customers where p95 must be low in multiple regions but model updates are centralized.

Decision rubric (quick checklist for SE workshop)
- If customer says "can’t send data to third-party": escalate to private path.
- If p95 requirement < 250ms and user base concentrated in specific region: prioritize dedicated in-region or edge placement.
- If QPS is bursty and cost is top constraint: recommend hosted initially while we quantify patterns; consider dedicated once stable.
- If procurement/contracting time >3 weeks and demo is urgent: hosted sandbox with data-masking and redaction.

Operational runbook (POC phases and concrete steps)
Phase 0 — Kickoff (0–3 days):
  - Confirm constraints (data residency, KYC, SLA).
  - Identify primary SLIs: p95 latency, error rate, token cost per request, model output QA pass rate.
  - Create shared workspace (Confluence + Slack channel).

Phase 1 — Fast proof (1–10 days): Hosted-first or hosted-masked
  - Provision API key, create test routes, set telemetry hooks.
  - Setup prompt guardrails (input redaction for PII), enable ephemeral logs.
  - Run smoke tests: latency baseline, cost per invocation estimate, simple eval prompts.
  - Deliver demo to customer; capture feedback and example bad prompts.

Phase 2 — Hardening (2–6 weeks): choose Dedicated or Hybrid
  - If moving to Dedicated: provision capacity, configure autoscale policies, set routing fallback to hosted.
  - If Hybrid: deploy edge cache or small private node, instrument prefix cache hit rate, configure split rules.
  - Add security integrations: customer KMS, VPC peering, audit sink.
  - Run load tests to confirm p95 and throughput targets.

Phase 3 — Private/on-prem (6–12+ weeks):
  - Pre-flight: infra checklist, approved AMIs/containers, network diagrams.
  - Install control plane (customer-managed routes), enable HSM/KMS rotation docs, hand off runbooks to customer ops.
  - Compliance audit run: evidence collection, attestation delivery.

Rollback and fallback strategies
- Always configure routing fallback to a compatible hosted model (lower capacity) with degraded SLA so customer app remains functional.
- Feature-flag model updates and rollout small % traffic first.
- For private nodes, keep a warm standby in dedicated pool to allow cross-fallthrough if connectivity drops.

Cost/latency heuristics (back-of-envelope)
- Hosted baseline: fastest to validate. Expect per-token unit costs to be higher for low volume but lower ops overhead. Latency depends on region-to-cloud hop; typical p95 100–400ms depending on payload.
- Dedicated: amortized cost becomes favorable at steady qps > ~30 sustained. Latency improves and becomes more stable; p95 commonly 60–200ms when colocated.
- Private on-prem: variable; can achieve single-digit ms for internal networks but ops cost and capital expense high.

Security & compliance checklist (minimum items for SE signoff)
- Identify data classification and required retention window.
- PII redaction or hashing steps in client.
- KMS integration plan and key rotation schedule.
- Audit log destination and retention policy.
- Network design: public IPs, peering, and firewall rules.
- Incident response contacts and escalation path.

Template: POC acceptance criteria (example)
- Functional: 90% of target user queries return results judged acceptable by customer sample set.
- Performance: p95 latency <= 350ms across 95% of test windows.
- Scalability: service handles 1.5x expected peak with <1% error.
- Security: PII masking present, audit logs shipped to customer SIEM.
- Cost: estimated monthly bill for selected topology within customer threshold (+/- 20%).

Known risks and mitigations
- Risk: Customer underestimates burstiness -> Mitigation: run burst tests, recommend burst capacity or queueing.
- Risk: Procurement delays for Dedicated/Private -> Mitigation: hosted sandbox with contractual notes.
- Risk: Poor eval prompts producing hallucinations -> Mitigation: prompt/response filters and small in-POC model tests.

Open questions to resolve in next workshop
- Does customer require encryption-in-use (HSM) or is encryption-at-rest adequate?
- Which regions must be supported from day one?
- Is there an existing SIEM and desired log format?

Quick checklist for the SE before handing to SRE/Infra:
- Clear topology chosen and documented (hosted | dedicated | private | hybrid).
- SLOs and acceptance criteria agreed and written down.
- Access model: API keys, service accounts, peering details documented.
- Data handling: PII redaction scripts or sample transformation included.
- Rollout plan and rollback triggers specified.

Appendix: brief example routing policy snippet (pseudocode)
  route_request(req):
    if req.customer_tier == "enterprise" and dedicated.available():
      return dedicated.endpoint(req)
    if cache.hit(req.prefix):
      return cache.serve(req)
    return hosted.fallback(req)

Next steps (recommended immediate actions)
1) Schedule 60-minute architecture workshop with customer to confirm constraints and demo hosted sandbox (Target: within 5 days).
2) Run synthetic latency/cost baseline on representative sample prompts (SE + infra, 2 days).
3) If regulated: start legal intake for private deployment scoping (SE + legal, 1 week).

Notes and provenance:
- This document synthesizes learnings from three mid-market POCs in H2 2024 and conversations with product infra teams about routing/fallback patterns.
- Keep iteration light — this note should be updated after each new POC to capture new edge cases.

Document owner and contact: Amira Khan (solutions-engineering) — ping in #se-hosting or email amira@redwood.ai for clarifications.
